figures.caption: Origin, physicochemical properties, and antimicrobial activity of encrypted peptides (EPs).(A) Normalized abundance of genes encoding proteins containing predicted EPs. The analysis was performed using the Panther Proteins Classification system with a false discovery rate cutoff of 0.05. (B) Tertiary structure of the host proteins and the selected encrypted peptides from six biogeographical areas: collagen (red), nervous system (orange), eye (yellow), tooth (light blue), immune system (blue), and leucine zipper (dark blue)-related proteins. (C) Comparison of the amino acid frequency in the EPs from this work, with human EPs and well-known antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) from databases. The amino acid counts were assessed using predicted EPs from the human proteome, natural and synthetic peptides from Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP), Antimicrobial Peptide Database (APD)-3, and Data Repository of Antimicrobial Peptides (DRAMP 3.0) (see also Figure S1A,B in the supplemental information online). The distribution is shown for two of the most important physicochemical features for their antimicrobial activity: (D) normalized hydrophobicity and (E) net charge of EPs from this work, EPs from the human proteome, and AMPs from databases (see also Figure S1C–H in the supplemental information online). Hydrophobicity directly influences the interactions of the peptide with lipids from the bacterial membrane, while net charge directly influences the initial electrostatic interactions between the peptide and negatively charged bacterial membranes. The hydrophobicity scale used to calculate the properties was the Eisenberg and Weiss consensus scale [62]. (F) Minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) values were obtained by testing peptide concentrations ranging from 0.78 to 50 μmol l−1 against 20 bacterial strains (seven pathogens and 13 human gut commensals). Reported data refer to assays carried out in triplicate and the heatmap shows the mode of MIC values collected from the experimental replicates. Figure created with BioRender (biorender.com). figures.caption: Secondary structure, resistance to proteolytic degradation, synergy, and mechanism of action of encrypted peptides (EPs).(A) Circular dichroism spectra of the most active EPs from various biogeographical areas and (B) percentage of secondary structure in trifluoroethanol and water mixture (3:2, v/v) [63,64] (see also Figure S2 in the supplemental information online). Unlike most of the active antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) [32,43,45], EP activity is not directly correlated with α-helical content. (C) The resistance to proteolytic degradation of representative EPs from each biogeographical area was assessed by exposing the peptides to human serum for 6 h. Aliquots of the resulting solution were analyzed by liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry; the most active peptides were those with higher resistance to proteolytic degradation. (D) The synergistic interaction between pairs of EPs from the same biogeographical area was analyzed by checkerboard assays with twofold serial dilutions starting at 2× minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) to MIC/32 against Acinetobacter baumannii. The histogram shows the fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) values obtained for each pair of EPs. Low FICI values (≤0.5) represent synergistic interactions, intermediary values (0.5<FICI≤1) and higher values represent indifferent (1<FICI≤2) and antagonistic (<2) interactions (see also Figure S3 in the supplemental information online). To assess whether EPs act on the bacterial membrane, all active EPs against A. baumannii ATCC 19606 were tested in outer membrane permeabilization and cytoplasmic membrane depolarization assays. The fluorescent probe 1-(N-phenylamino)naphthalene (NPN) was used to indicate membrane permeabilization (E) caused by the EPs tested (see also Figure S4 in the supplemental information online). The fluorescent probe 3,3′-dipropylthiadicarbocyanine iodide (DiSC3-5) was used to indicate membrane depolarization (F) caused by collagenins, neuronins, eyesins, toothins, immunosins, and zipperins (see also Figure S5 in the supplemental information online). The values shown represent the relative fluorescence of both probes used as a nonlinear fitting using as baseline the untreated control (buffer + bacteria + fluorescent dye) in comparison to polymyxin B, an antibiotic known for its permeabilization properties that also shows some depolarizing activity. All experiments were performed in three independent replicates.

figures.caption: Cytotoxicity and immunomodulatory properties of encrypted peptides (EPs).(A) Schematic of a skin wound infection triggering an inflammatory response. Correlations between cytotoxicity and antimicrobial activity [expressed as minimal inhibitory concentration for complete bacterial killing (MIC100)] are shown in scatter plots. The impact on (B) red blood cells (RBCs) in terms of hemolytic effects, and cytotoxicity for (C) immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT) and (D) PMA-differentiated human monocytes (THP-1) are expressed using predicted hemolytic concentrations leading to 50% cell death (HC50) and cytotoxic concentrations leading to 50% cell death (CC50) values. HC50 and CC50 values were obtained through interpolation of the dose response using a nonlinear regression curve (see also Figure S6 in the supplemental information online). The release of proinflammatory markers from (E) HaCaT and (F) PMA-differentiated THP-1 cells, whether uninfected or infected with live or heat-killed Acinetobacter baumannii, was examined after a 20-h treatment with each EP. Samples were collected and analyzed to detect levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). Data are shown as mean of two independent experiments (in quadruplicate) for each group (see also Figures S7–S10 in the supplemental information online). Figure created with BioRender (biorender.com). Abbreviation: MOI, multiplicity of infection.

figures.caption: Anti-infective activity of encrypted peptides (EPs) in preclinical animal models.(A) Schematic of the skin abscess infection mouse model used to assess the anti-infective activity of the collagenins against Acinetobacter baumannii in wounded epidermis. In this model, mice had their back shaved, wounded, and infected with A. baumannii. They were treated 1 h post infection with a single dose of the collagenins at their minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for A. baumannii ATCC 19606. (B) Weight changes were used as a proxy for toxicity of the EPs throughout the experiment. We considered up to 20% weight change as the threshold for lack of toxicity. (C) Mice were euthanized 2 or 4 days post infection. Each group (treated and untreated) comprised three mice (N = 3) and the bacterial loads used for infection of each mouse came from different inocula grown and prepared independently. Collagenin-3 presented bactericidal effects comparable with those of the positive control antibiotic, polymyxin-B. Collagenins 4, 5, and 7 had bacteriostatic effect 2 days after infection. Four days post infection, the only peptides that did not allow proliferation of A. baumannii were collagenins 3 and 4 (see also Figure S11 in the supplemental information online). (D) Schematic of the deep thigh infection mouse model used to assess the anti-infective activity of immunosins and zipperins against A. baumannii in an intramuscular infection. In this model, mice were first rendered neutropenic by two rounds of treatment of cyclophosphamide. Subsequently, bacterial cells were injected intramuscularly in the right thigh followed by the intraperitoneal administration of a single dose of one of the two families of EPs at their MIC against A. baumannii. Two days post infection (6 days after the start of the experiment), mice were euthanized. Each group had three subjects (N = 3), with independently prepared bacterial loads. (E) Weight changes were monitored throughout the experiment. (F) Except for immunosin-1, all peptides tested were active. Immunosins 2, 7, and 11 showed bacteriostatic activity, while immunosins 3, 12, and 13 and zipperins 1 and 2 had bactericidal activity comparable with that observed for polymyxin-B. Levofloxacin, another antibiotic used as positive control, was the most active compound tested, leading to clearance or significant reduction of the bacterial load. One-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test was used to determine statistical significance in (C,F), and the P-values are presented for each group. All groups were compared with the untreated control, and the violin plots display the median and upper and lower quartiles. Data in (B,E) are the mean plus and minus the standard deviation. Figure created with BioRender (biorender.com). Abbreviation: CFU, colony-forming unit.
